sections.h2: What does selling a house in New York City involve that other places do not?
sections.html:
New York City is five boroughs and five counties, so the paperwork for a sale depends on which borough the house is in. Manhattan is New York County, Brooklyn is Kings, Queens and the Bronx share their county names, and Staten Island is Richmond County.

The city is also a municipality with its own real property transfer tax, its own property tax classes and its own Department of Finance. A house of up to three units is a Class 1 property, which sets its tax rate and appeal deadline, while co-ops and most condominiums fall in Class 2. This page focuses on houses rather than co-op shares.

The Census Bureau estimates 8,584,629 residents for July 1, 2025, down 2.5 percent from the 2020 estimates base, spread over about 300 square miles of land at 29,303 people per square mile.

sections.h2: How do the five boroughs differ for a house seller?
sections.html:
Each borough has its own character and its own mix of house types. Staten Island is the most suburban and calls itself the Borough of Parks, with about 12,300 acres of protected parkland. The Bronx is the only borough on the mainland and has the city's largest park, Pelham Bay Park, at 2,772 acres. Queens is the largest borough by area and holds both JFK and LaGuardia airports.

Brooklyn is the most populous borough and has a long beachfront, including Coney Island. Manhattan is the smallest and densest, with a density above 70,000 people per square mile.

  • Staten Island: Richmond County, linked to Brooklyn by the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge and to Manhattan by the free ferry
  • The Bronx: Bronx County, home of Co-op City, the largest cooperatively owned housing complex in the country
  • Queens: Queens County, on Long Island north and east of Brooklyn
  • Brooklyn: Kings County, on the western tip of Long Island

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about homeownership in New York City?
sections.html:
Fewer than one in three households in the city owns its home. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 32.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, with a median home value of $777,600 and a median gross rent of $1,821.

That makes the city a renter-heavy market, and houses a smaller slice of it. There are 3,334,088 households, averaging 2.48 people, and the median household income is $80,483 in 2024 dollars. Foreign-born residents make up 36.6 percent of the population, and 47.7 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home.

Mean travel time to work is 40.3 minutes, the longest of the four places in the Census comparison. For a seller of a house near a subway stop or a rail line, transit access is a selling point worth putting in the first line of the listing.

sections.h2: How does New York City property tax work for a one, two or three-family house?
sections.html:
The city's property tax year runs July 1 to June 30, and what you owe depends on the tax class and assessed value. A property with an assessed value of $250,000 or less gets quarterly bills, and one above that gets semiannual bills.

Tax classWhat it covers2026 rate
Class 1Most residential property of up to three units19.843%
Class 2Other primarily residential property, such as co-ops and condos12.439%
Class 3Property with gas, telephone or electric company equipment11.108%
Class 4All other property, such as offices and warehouses10.848%

Source: NYC Department of Finance property tax rates page.

Quarterly payers owe on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, with a 15-day grace period. Semiannual payers owe on July 1 and January 1. Paying the full year by the July due date earns a 0.50 percent discount, and interest on late payments compounds daily. If a bill is still open when you sell, ask your closing attorney how it will be handled at closing.

sections.h2: How do I challenge my New York City assessment before I sell?
sections.html:
You appeal to the NYC Tax Commission, an independent agency, and the deadline for a Class 1 house is March 15. Classes 2, 3 and 4 have an earlier March 1 deadline, and late appeals are not granted. The Tax Commission can lower the assessment, change the tax class and adjust exemptions.

The Department of Finance runs a separate path: a Request for Review to fix a property description or clerical error is due March 15 for Class 1 and April 1 for other properties. A Request for Review does not replace a Tax Commission appeal, so file both if you need both.

A lower assessment helps a buyer's budget as well as yours. If you are listing a house in the spring, check whether the deadline has already passed this cycle.

For high-value homes, a new surcharge on some non-primary residences also applies. A law in effect since May 28, 2026 charges one, two and three-family homes valued at $5 million or more 0.8 percent of market value, rising to 1.05 and 1.3 percent at higher values. It does not apply to a house used as a primary residence by the owner, a tenant or a family member. The exemption application deadline for 2026-27 was October 13, 2026, and any charges appear on the bill due January 1, 2027.

sections.h2: What taxes come out of the sale price in New York City?
sections.html:
The seller pays the New York State transfer tax, and the city adds its own real property transfer tax, which is usually settled with the other closing costs. The state tax is $2 for each $500 of the price. For a city conveyance of residential property at $3 million or more, the state adds $1.25 for each $500, also paid by the seller.

The buyer pays the 1 percent mansion tax on residences of $1 million or more, and a supplemental tax of 0.25 to 2.9 percent when the price is $2 million or more. The city's own tax is filed on Form NYC-RPT, created online through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. Both the seller and the buyer must sign it, and late filing adds 5 percent of the tax for each month, up to 25 percent.

Ask your closing attorney for the exact city figure, since it depends on the type of transfer and the price. If you are a nonresident of New York State, you must compute your gain and pay any estimated income tax unless an exemption on Form TP-584-NYC applies.

sections.h2: Why does the certificate of occupancy matter when selling a New York City house?
sections.html:
A certificate of occupancy states the legal use of a building, and no one may legally occupy a building until the Department of Buildings has issued one or a temporary certificate (TCO). It has no expiration date, but you cannot get one while there are open applications or open violations on the property.

Buildings put up or altered before 1938 may not need one. In that case, a Letter of No Objection from the borough office can prove the legal use. Search your address in DOB NOW to see whether a certificate is on file.

The Department advises buyers to negotiate on a final certificate, not a temporary one. A temporary certificate that has expired and not been renewed can make a house hard to insure, sell or refinance. If you built an extension or finished a basement without closing out the job, a cash buyer who takes the house as-is will price that in, so fix or disclose it before you take the offer.

faqs.q: When are New York City property tax bills due?
faqs.a: On July 1 and January 1 for semiannual payers, and also October 1 and April 1 for quarterly payers. Quarterly bills have a grace period through the 15th of the month.

faqs.q: What is the property tax rate for a one-family house in New York City?
faqs.a: The Department of Finance sets the Class 1 rate at 19.843 percent for tax year 2026. Class 1 covers most residential property of up to three units, so a one-family house falls in it.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a New York City house assessment?
faqs.a: March 15 for Class 1 properties, filed with the NYC Tax Commission. Class 2, 3 and 4 properties must file by March 1.

faqs.q: Who pays the New York State transfer tax in a city sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays the base tax of $2 per $500 of the price, unless the contract says otherwise. The buyer pays the mansion tax if the price is $1 million or more.

faqs.q: Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell a house in New York City?
faqs.a: Not always. Houses built before 1938 may lack one, and a Letter of No Objection from the Department of Buildings can show the legal use. For anything newer or altered, the buyer's attorney will ask for the certificate.
